entries.knownHazards: Although no specific mention has been seen for this species, it belongs to a genus where most, if not all members of the genus produce hydrogen cyanide, a poison that gives almonds their characteristic flavour. This toxin is found mainly in the leaves and seed and is readily detected by its bitter taste. It is usually present in too small a quantity to do any harm but any very bitter seed or fruit should not be eaten. In small quantities, hydrogen cyanide has been shown to stimulate respiration and improve digestion, it is also claimed to be of benefit in the treatment of cancer. In excess, however, it can cause respiratory failure and even death.

This toxin is found mainly in the leaves and seed and is readily detected by its bitter taste. It is usually present in too small a quantity to do any harm but any very bitter seed or fruit should not be eaten. In small quantities, hydrogen cyanide has been shown to stimulate respiration and improve digestion, it is also claimed to be of benefit in the treatment of cancer. In excess, however, it can cause respiratory failure and even death.

entries.knownHazards: There are a number of reports regarding the possible health risks of this plant. The huge quantity of spores released by large areas of bracken are suggested to be implicated in stomach cancers. A recent study suggests that this is not such a problem in Britain as was once believed, the spores are not produced in such high quantities nor do they travel so far due to our normally humid atmosphere. The leaves and roots contain substances that deprive the body of vitamin B1 if they are eaten raw, though they are possibly alright cooked[102]. The leaves are also said to be be carcinogenic[65, 76].

entries.knownHazards: Weak skin sensitizing effects. May cause diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting. Not suitable for long term use. Reduces mineral absorption from gut [301].
entries.knownHazardsLtV2: Gali dirginti odą, sukelti viduriavimą, pykinimą ir vėmimą. Netinka ilgalaikiam vartojimui — mažina mineralų įsisavinimą žarnyne.

entries.flagReason: FACT FIDELITY: EN says 'Weak skin sensitizing effects' — this means potential to cause allergic sensitization (sensitization ≠ irritation). LT 'gali dirginti odą' (may irritate skin) translates as irritant effect, not sensitizing effect. 'Dirginti' implies acute/direct irritation; sensitization implies immunological reaction potential on repeated exposure. The distinction matters for safety labeling. Suggested LT: 'gali jautrinti odą' (sensitize) or 'gali sukelti odos jautrumą'.
entries.suggestedFix: Replace 'Gali dirginti odą' with 'Gali jautrinti odą' (sensitizing) or 'Gali sukelti odos jautrumą (jautrinantis poveikis)' to accurately convey sensitization rather than simple irritation.

entries.knownHazards: All parts of the plant contain tannins. Whilst tannins are found in many foods, and have a range of medicinal uses. They are usually only present in low concentrations. In some foods made from oaks (particularly the seeds), the tannin content can be quite high unless the food is treated to reduce tannin content. Tannins are only of low toxicity and, because of their bitter taste and astringency, are unlikely to be eaten in large quantities. However, if they are taken in excess, they can cause stomach pains; constipation followed by bloody diarrhoea: excessive thirst; and excessive urination[293].

entries.flagReason: GRAMMAR: 'sultys' (sap/juice) in Lithuanian is feminine gender (mot. g.), not masculine. The changesNotes incorrectly state 'sultys — vyr. g. daugiskaita' (masculine plural). The correct adjective agreement for feminine plural 'sultys' is 'aštrios' (not 'aštrūs'). The edited form 'Aštrūs augalo sultys' introduces a new gender agreement error. Additionally, LT 'dirgina odą' does not fully convey EN 'cause blistering' — blistering is more severe than irritation ('sukelia pūsles' correctly captures blistering, so this part is fine).
entries.suggestedFix: Correct adjective gender: 'Aštrios augalo sultys dirgina odą ir sukelia pūsles.' ('sultys' is feminine in Lithuanian; correct agreement is 'aštrios' not 'aštrūs').
